theme: He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High, under God’s wings
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 91. It is one of the best-loved psalms in the Bible, and it fits the end of a long study of the tabernacle. Read it as a description of what it means to live in God’s presence.
settingTheScene: Psalm 91 has no title in the Hebrew, and its author is not named. Jewish tradition connects it with Moses, because the previous psalm, Psalm 90, is “A Prayer of Moses.” The psalm is a song of trust. It speaks first about dwelling in the shelter of the Most High, then switches to a promise spoken to the believer, and ends with the voice of God himself. After the reading of the tabernacle, with the glory-cloud, the wings of the cherubim on the ark, and the presence of God among his people, this psalm applies those images to the believer’s life.
observation: “He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty” (v. 1).
“I will say to the LORD, My refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust” (v. 2).
“He will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge; his faithfulness is a shield and buckler” (v. 4).
The believer need not fear “the terror of the night,” “the arrow that flies by day,” “the pestilence,” or “the destruction that wastes at noonday” (vv. 5-6).
“A thousand may fall at your side, ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not come near you” (v. 7).
“For he will command his angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways” (v. 11).
“Because he holds fast to me in love, I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he knows my name” (v. 14).
“With long life I will satisfy him and show him my salvation” (v. 16).
interpretation:
The images of the psalm come from the tabernacle. “Shelter” and “shadow” recall the tent. “Under his wings” recalls the cherubim whose wings covered the mercy seat. The one who “dwells” in the shelter of the Most High is a person who lives in his presence. It is a picture of the believer as someone who has taken up residence in God’s house.

The promises that follow are bold. God will protect from plague, from enemies, and from danger. It is important to read them correctly. The Bible does not teach that believers will never suffer, and the psalm itself acknowledges that thousands may fall. The Bible also shows faithful people suffering, including Job, the prophets, and the apostles. The promise is not that nothing will touch you. It is that nothing will touch you apart from God. His presence is with you in the fire and the flood.

This is the lesson Satan missed when he quoted verses 11 and 12 to Jesus in the wilderness (Matthew 4:6). He took the promise of protection and tried to turn it into a license to test God. Jesus answered by quoting Deuteronomy: “You shall not put the LORD your God to the test.” The psalm is a promise to be trusted, not a tool for demanding proof.

The last three verses are spoken by God himself. “Because he holds fast to me in love, I will deliver him.” Notice the reason: not that the person is perfect, but that he holds fast. God’s love and the believer’s trust come together. “I will be with him in trouble; I will rescue him and honor him.” The deepest promise is the presence of God in trouble.

At the end, he says, “I will show him my salvation.” The word is yeshuah, the root of the name of Jesus. The psalm ends with the promise of salvation, which is finally a person.
connection: Jesus used the image of a hen gathering her chicks under her wings (Matthew 23:37). Paul says, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” and that nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:31-39). Hebrews 1:14 says that angels are “ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation.” Jesus, the one who knew the Father’s name perfectly, is our refuge, and in him we dwell.
application:
Say aloud verses 1 and 2 as a personal declaration. Consider what it means to “dwell” in God’s shelter, not just visit it.

Think of a fear you have. Place it before the Lord and ask him to be your refuge in it.

Do not use this psalm to demand something from God. Use it to trust him.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you want to hold on to him in.
Thank him for his presence in every trouble.
Ask him to show you his salvation in Jesus.
